claim: Central pattern generators (CPGs) are neurons or neural circuits that produce periodic output without requiring patterned input.
source: Central pattern generators (CPGs) are neurons or neural circuits that produce periodic output without requiring patterned input.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided in the abstract that establishes what CPGs are.

claim: Nested CPGs have been proposed to coordinate repetitive elements of complex behaviors, organizing control over different time scales.
source: More complex behaviors can be assembled from simpler subroutines, and nested CPGs have been proposed to coordinate their repetitive elements, organizing control over different time scales.
evidence: This statement references the concept of nested CPGs as a proposed framework in the field.

claim: Drosophila grooming involves periodic leg sweeps and rubs on a short time scale of 5–7 Hz (~200 ms/movement).
source: On a short time scale (5–7 Hz, ~ 200 ms/movement), flies clean with periodic leg sweeps and rubs.
evidence: The abstract directly states the frequency and period of short time scale movements.

claim: Transitions between bouts of head sweeping and leg rubbing in Drosophila grooming are periodic on a longer time scale of 0.3–0.6 Hz (~2 s/bout).
source: More surprisingly, transitions between bouts of head sweeping and leg rubbing are also periodic on a longer time scale (0.3–0.6 Hz, ~2 s/bout).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the frequency and period of long time scale oscillations.

claim: The frequencies of both short and long time scale oscillations in Drosophila grooming increase with temperature.
source: We examine grooming at a range of temperatures to show that the frequencies of both oscillations increase—a hallmark of CPG control
evidence: The abstract states that both oscillation frequencies increase with temperature, which is demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Temperature-dependent frequency increase is a hallmark of CPG control.
source: We examine grooming at a range of temperatures to show that the frequencies of both oscillations increase—a hallmark of CPG control
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CPG characteristics.

claim: The rhythms at the two time scales increase at the same rate, indicating that the nested CPGs may be linked.
source: rhythms at the two time scales increase at the same rate, indicating that the nested CPGs may be linked.
evidence: The abstract states this relationship and provides it as evidence for linkage between CPGs.

claim: The relationship between the two time scales holds when sensory drive is held constant using optogenetic activation.
source: This relationship holds when sensory drive is held constant using optogenetic activation
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental finding.

claim: Oscillations can decouple in spontaneously grooming flies, showing that alternative control modes are possible.
source: but oscillations can decouple in spontaneously grooming flies, showing that alternative control modes are possible.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation and its interpretation.

claim: Loss of sensory feedback does not disrupt periodicity but slows down the longer time scale alternation.
source: Loss of sensory feedback does not disrupt periodicity but slow down the longer time scale alternation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental finding.

claim: CPGs control short stereotypic actions in cat walking, crayfish swimming, locust flight, leech heartbeat, and the stomatogastric and pyloric rhythms of crustaceans.
source: CPGs control short stereotypic actions in cat walking, crayfish swimming, locust flight, leech heartbeat, and the stomatogastric and pyloric rhythms of crustaceans (reviewed in Berkowitz, 2019; Harris-Warrick and Ramirez, 2017 ; Grillner, 2006; Marder and Calabrese, 1996; Mulloney and Smarandache, 2010; Selverston, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: When flies are covered in dust, they initially groom anterior body parts using their front legs.
source: When flies are covered in dust, they initially groom anterior body parts using their front legs (Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Seeds et al., 2014.

claim: Flies alternate between bouts of head sweeps, where the legs move synchronously, and bouts of leg rubbing, where the legs move in opposition to each other.
source: They alternate between bouts of head sweeps, where the legs move synchronously, and bouts of leg rubbing, where the legs move in opposition to each other, scraping the dust off.
evidence: This is a direct observation described in the results section.

claim: At 18°C, leg rubs and sweeps have a characteristic frequency of approximately 6 Hz.
source: At 18°C, leg rubs and sweeps have a characteristic frequency ~6 Hz.
evidence: This is stated as a measured frequency from the data.

claim: Each leg movement takes approximately 150 ms to complete at 18°C.
source: This means that each leg movement takes approximately 150 ms to complete, which is consistent with our observations using higher resolution video recordings (see below).
evidence: This is calculated from the frequency data and confirmed by high-resolution video.

claim: The alternation of head cleaning and front leg rubbing bouts is periodic with a frequency of approximately 0.33 Hz at 18°C.
source: Autocorrelation analysis of the time series shown in Figure 1H illustrates signal at ~0.33 Hz, corresponding to approximately 2 s between the mid-point of consecutive bouts of front leg rubbing.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: Head sweeps and leg rubbing movements of dusted flies grooming at 18°C have a mean Periodicity Index (PI) of 0.31.
source: Using this metric, head sweeps and leg rubbing movements of dusted flies grooming at 18°C have a mean PI of 0.31 (s.d.=0.02) and 0.31 (s.d.=0.01), respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported from the data.

claim: The alternation between bouts (the long time scale) at 18°C has a mean Periodicity Index of 0.36.
source: the alternation between bouts (the long time scale) at 18°C has a mean PI of 0.36 (s.d.=0.02).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported from the data.

claim: The amount of periodic behavior for the long time scale is 80% at 18°C.
source: Using these ratios, we found that overall the amount of periodic behavior for the long time scale is 80% (s.d.=8%) at 18°C.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported from the data.

claim: A key feature of CPGs is that they oscillate faster at higher temperatures.
source: A key feature of CPGs is that they oscillate faster at higher temperatures (Deliagina et al., 1983; Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of individual leg movements increases linearly with temperature from 5.7 Hz to 6.6 Hz (R2=0.99, p<0.001).
source: the frequency shows a linear increase from 5.7 Hz to 6.6 Hz (R2=0.99, p<0.001; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the temperature manipulation experiment, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The ff/hh-cycle frequency increases from 0.42 Hz at 18°C to 0.49 Hz at 30°C in a linear manner (R2=0.96, p<0.001).
source: The ff/hh-cycle frequency increases from 0.42 Hz (s.d.=0.02) at 18°C to 0.49 Hz (s.d.=0.04) at 30°C, also in a linear manner (R2=0.96, p<0.001; Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the temperature manipulation experiment, with reference to Figure 2F-H.

claim: The average number of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle is fairly consistent, averaging approximately 15 across temperatures.
source: We noticed that the number of leg movements within an ff/hh-cycle is fairly consistent, averaging ~15: means range from 13.2 to 15.8 and s.d. range from 0.75 to 1.95 across temperatures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: At 18°C, there are 15 leg movements of 175 ms for an ff/hh-cycle duration of 2.38 s.
source: At 18°C, there are 15 leg movements of 175 ms for an ff/hh-cycle duration of 2.38 s
evidence: This is a specific calculation from the data at 18°C.

claim: At 30°C, there are 15 leg movements of 152 ms for an ff/hh-cycle duration of 2.04 s.
source: while at 30°C there are 15 leg movements of 152 ms for an ff/hh-cycle duration of 2.04 s.
evidence: This is a specific calculation from the data at 30°C.

claim: The average number of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle remains constant even as the cycle duration shortens with increasing temperature.
source: Thus, the average number of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle remains constant even as the cycle duration shortens with increasing temperature (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing the relationship between temperature and cycle composition.

claim: The correlation between the contraction rates of the two time scales is striking (R2=0.96, p<0.001).
source: Normalizing by their minimal frequencies, we can visualize the slope of temperature dependence for each time scale and the correlation between them is striking (R2=0.96, p<0.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing the correlation between the two time scales.

claim: Both time scales contract at the same rate, with R2 values of 0.995 and 0.956, respectively.
source: Both time scales contract at the same rate, with R2 values of 0.995 and 0.956, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical result quantifying the rate of contraction for each time scale.

claim: An additional criterion for determining if a behavior is controlled by a CPG is that rhythmic output does not require rhythmic input.
source: An additional criterion for determining if a behavior is controlled by a CPG is that rhythmic output does not require rhythmic input.
evidence: This is stated as an established criterion for CPG identification.

claim: Optogenetic activation of mechanosensory bristle neurons induces grooming, beginning with the anterior body parts, and causing alternation between bouts of head cleaning and front leg rubbing.
source: We previously demonstrated that this manipulation induces grooming, beginning with the anterior body parts, and causing alternation between bouts of head cleaning and front leg rubbing (Hampel et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a previously demonstrated result, supported by citations.

claim: Under optogenetic activation, both individual leg movements and bout-level alternations increase in frequency with temperature and do so in a correlated manner.
source: Here, we combine optogenetic activation for constant sensory input with changing temperature to show that both individual leg movements and bout-level alternations increase in frequency with temperature and that they do so in a correlated manner.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The PIs at 18°C for short and long time scales under optogenetic stimulation are 0.29 and 0.35, respectively.
source: For example, the PIs at 18°C for short and long time scales are 0.29 (s.d.=0.03) and 0.35 (s.d.=0.03), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The amount of periodic behavior for the long time scale under optogenetic stimulation is 62% at 18°C.
source: and the amount of periodic behavior, considering the long time scale alterations, is 62% (s.d.=10%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The amount of periodic behavior under optogenetic stimulation (62%) is less than in dusted flies (80%).
source: This amount of periodic behavior is less than the 80% (s.d.=8%) in the dusted flies
evidence: This is a comparison between two experimental conditions.

claim: Sensory feedback may be needed to stabilize rhythms but not necessarily to generate them in the first place.
source: We propose that sensory feedback may be needed to stabilize rhythms but not necessarily to generate them in the first place.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The frequencies of optogenetically induced rhythms get shorter with temperature.
source: The period of the optogenetically induced rhythms gets shorter with temperature (Figure 4C–H).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The average number of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle is preserved across the range of temperatures under optogenetic stimulation.
source: The frequencies are similar to dust-induced grooming, and the average number of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle is also preserved across the range of temperatures (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The rate of contraction of the two time scales is correlated under optogenetic stimulation.
source: As with dusted flies, the rate of contraction of the two time scales is correlated (Figure 4K)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Movements of both the intact leg and the stump remained periodic after leg amputation, with frequencies and PIs similar to those of intact legs in dusted flies.
source: We found that movements of both the intact leg and the stump remained periodic, with frequencies and PIs similar to those of intact legs in dusted flies.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the leg amputation experiments.

claim: The frequency of rubs is lower in the TNT group than in the control (p< 0.001).
source: The frequency of rubs is lower in the TNT group than in the control (p< 0.001) (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: The frequency of sweeps is similar for both TNT and control groups.
source: while the frequency of sweeps is similar for both (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: The long time scale oscillations are significantly slower in the TNT group (p<0.003).
source: The long time scale oscillations are significantly slower in the TNT group (p<0.003) (Figure 5H, also ethograms in Figure 5A)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: The numbers of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle are slower in the TNT group.
source: and so are the numbers of leg movements per ff/hh-cycle (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: Both TNT and control groups exhibited periodic behaviors on both the long and short time scales.
source: Both groups exhibited periodic behaviors on both the long and short time scales (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: The sensory inhibited flies performed less overall periodic behavior on the long time scale.
source: The sensory inhibited flies also performed less overall periodic behavior on the long time scale (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the TNT inhibition experiments.

claim: Grooming behaviors do not require sensory input for periodicity, but do utilize it for timing, modulation, and perhaps stabilization of the motor output, especially on the longer time scale.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that grooming behaviors do not require sensory input for periodicity, but do utilize it for timing, modulation, and perhaps stabilization of the motor output, especially on the longer time scale.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from the sensory manipulation experiments.

claim: Spontaneous grooming shows less periodicity at the long time scale than dust-induced grooming.
source: Our observation that spontaneous grooming shows less periodicity at the long time scale (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) can be interpreted as effective decoupling of the two levels of the nested CPG in those flies when they engage in more sporadic and shorter episodes of grooming.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the spontaneous grooming experiments.

claim: In spontaneously grooming flies, the temperature-dependent contraction of the long time scale is less pronounced than in the stimulated flies (R2=0.86; p=0.012).
source: The ff/hh-cycles are rarer, and when they occur, the temperature-dependent contraction of the long time scale is less pronounced than in the stimulated flies (R2=0.86; p=0.012) (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spontaneous grooming experiments.

claim: The correlated temperature-dependent contraction of the short and long time scales observed in the dusted and optogenetically activated flies is not seen in the spontaneously grooming ones (R2=0.43; p=0.332).
source: the correlated temperature-dependent contraction of the short and long time scales observed in the dusted and optogenetically activated flies is not seen in the spontaneously grooming ones (R2=0.43; p=0.332) (compare Figure 6K to Figures 3K and 4K).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing spontaneous grooming to other conditions.

claim: The frequency of leg rubs and sweeps increases with temperature at a greater rate than the frequency of ff/hh-cycles in spontaneously grooming flies.
source: The frequency of leg rubs and sweeps increases with temperature at a greater rate than the frequency of ff/hh-cycles (Figure 6K), suggesting that the pattern-generating circuits that control the two time scales of movements may be dissociated in spontaneous grooming.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the spontaneous grooming experiments.

claim: Neither periodic nor non-periodic behaviors in spontaneously grooming flies changed frequency with temperature.
source: However, we found that neither periodic nor non-periodic behaviors changed frequency with temperature (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This is stated as a result from analyzing periodic vs non-periodic spontaneous grooming.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the two time scales in spontaneously grooming flies.
source: and there was no significant correlation between the two time scales (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F), or between the two levels of the nested CPG, in spontaneously grooming flies.
evidence: This is stated as a result from analyzing spontaneous grooming.

claim: Local cooling of the cat spinal cord demonstrated which segments contain locomotion control circuits.
source: Local cooling of the cat spinal cord demonstrated which segments contain locomotion control circuits (Deliagina et al., 1983)
evidence: This is stated as an established finding supported by a citation.

claim: Local warming showed that cricket chirping is governed by thoracic rather than brain ganglia.
source: and local warming showed that cricket chirping is governed by thoracic rather than brain ganglia (Pires and Hoy, 1992a; Pires and Hoy, 1992b).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding supported by citations.

claim: Local cooling of the HVC brain region in birds expands the entire song without changing the relative durations of the syllables and sub-syllabic components.
source: The role of CPGs in bird song, and the importance of the HVC brain region for sequence timing, was shown because local cooling expands the entire song without changing the relative durations of the syllables and sub-syllabic components (Armstrong and Abarbanel, 2016; Long and Fee, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding supported by citations.

claim: In frogs (Xenopus laevis), both local cooling and ambient temperature affect the frequencies of vocalization patterns.
source: In frogs (Xenopus laevis), both local cooling and ambient temperature affect the frequencies of vocalization patterns (Yamaguchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established finding supported by a citation.

claim: Fly grooming is an innate motor sequence with both repetition and flexibility.
source: Fly grooming is an innate motor sequence with both repetition and flexibility.
evidence: This is a characterization of fly grooming behavior.

claim: Behavior analysis has shown organization over several time scales in fly grooming, from single stereotyped leg movements and alternations between bouts of repeated actions targeting specific body parts, to a gradual and probabilistic progression from anterior toward posterior grooming.
source: Behavior analysis has shown organization over several time scales, from single stereotyped leg movements and alternations between bouts of repeated actions targeting specific body parts (Mueller et al., 2019), to a gradual and probabilistic progression from anterior toward posterior grooming (Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The neural circuits that constitute the CPGs controlling periodic leg movements are likely to overlap with those proposed to coordinate walking.
source: Since the neural circuits that constitute the CPGs controlling these periodic leg movements are likely to overlap with those proposed to coordinate walking (Bidaye et al., 2018), this was not unexpected.
evidence: This is stated as a reasonable expectation based on cited work.

claim: CPGs may control each leg joint, regulating the interaction between flexor and extensor muscles, governing the way coxa-trochanter and femur-tibia joints are coordinated to produce forward or backward walking, or mediating interactions among limbs.
source: CPGs may control each leg joint, regulating the interaction between flexor and extensor muscles, governing the way coxa-trochanter and femur-tibia joints are coordinated to produce forward or backward walking, or mediating interactions among limbs (Feng et al., 2020; Mantziaris et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the vertebrate spinal cord, inhibitory and excitatory commissural neurons can cause the CPGs controlling the legs to synchronize for a hopping gait or operate out-of-phase for walking.
source: In the vertebrate spinal cord, inhibitory and excitatory commissural neurons can cause the CPGs controlling the legs to synchronize for a hopping gait or operate out-of-phase for walking (Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CPGs in frogs have been shown to act on different time scales (sequentially) to govern their vocal behaviors.
source: CPGs in frogs have been shown to act on different time scales (sequentially) to govern their vocal behaviors (Zornik et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Leeches can alternate between different CPG-driven behaviors.
source: and leeches can alternate between different CPG-driven behaviors (Esch et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The concept of nested CPGs has recently been extended to explain the flexible coordination of behaviors ranging from fish swimming to bird song.
source: The concept of nested CPGs has recently been extended to explain the flexible coordination of behaviors ranging from fish swimming to bird song (Berkowitz, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as recent work supported by a citation.

claim: Nested CPGs similar to the one proposed for fly grooming have been described in the crab stomatogastric ganglion, where fast pyloric and slow gastric mill rhythms are coupled and compensate for temperature changes.
source: In a recent publication, nested CPGs similar to the one we are proposing here have been described in the crab stomatogastric ganglion, where fast pyloric and slow gastric mill rhythms are coupled and compensate for temperature changes (Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding supported by a citation.

claim: The phase of different components of CPGs is conserved across a range of temperatures.
source: Just as the relative number of rotations between different gears is the same regardless of the absolute speed of the mechanism, so the phase of different components of CPGs is conserved across a range of temperatures (Harris-Warrick and Ramirez, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Disturbing a single bristle elicits a single directed leg sweep.
source: Disturbing a single bristle elicits a single directed leg sweep (Kays et al., 2014; Vandervorst and Ghysen, 1980)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Covering the fly in dust evokes an entire grooming program with bouts of several leg sweeps and rubs, alternation between the bouts, and slow gradual anterior-to-posterior progression.
source: while covering the fly in dust evokes an entire grooming program with bouts of several leg sweeps and rubs, alternation between the bouts, and slow gradual anterior-to-posterior progression (Phillis et al., 1993; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sensory feedback plays a role in stabilizing and adjusting rhythmic behaviors in walking mice.
source: The concept of sensory feedback playing a role in stabilizing and adjusting rhythmic behaviors has been explored in walking mice (Mayer and Akay, 2018, Santuz et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sensory feedback plays a role in stabilizing and adjusting rhythmic behaviors in walking flies.
source: and flies (Mendes et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The complete electron microscopy data set covering the ventral nerve cord will enable the identification of the pre-motor neurons most likely to participate in CPGs and the commissural connections that may mediate among them.
source: New anatomical resources to map neural circuits, especially the complete electron microscopy data set covering the ventral nerve cord (Phelps et al., 2021), will enable the identification of the pre-motor neurons most likely to participate in CPGs and the commissural connections that may mediate among them.
evidence: This is a statement about future possibilities based on new resources.

claim: Functional imaging of neural activity in dissected, fictive preparations is a promising approach to identify neurons with rhythmic activity that may constitute parts of the CPGs.
source: Functional imaging of neural activity in dissected, fictive preparations (Pulver et al., 2015) and even in behaving flies (Chen et al., 2018) is another promising approach to identify neurons with rhythmic activity that may constitute parts of the CPGs.
evidence: This is a statement about promising approaches supported by citations.

claim: Whole nervous system monitoring of neural activity was recently described in C. elegans to identify hierarchical and dynamic control of nested locomotion patterns.
source: For example, whole nervous system monitoring of neural activity was recently described in C. elegans to identify hierarchical and dynamic control of nested locomotion patterns (Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding supported by a citation.

claim: Identifying what circuits constitute the grooming CPGs and mapping the neurons that coordinate their interactions is feasible.
source: Identifying what circuits constitute these CPGs and mapping the neurons that coordinate their interactions is feasible, now that we know we ought to be looking for them.
evidence: This is a statement about the feasibility of future research based on the current findings.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster was reared on common cornmeal food in a 25°C incubator on a 12-hr light/dark cycle.
source: Drosophila melanogaster was reared on common cornmeal food in a 25°C incubator on a 12-hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Three to five days old CantonS males were used for dusting and spontaneous grooming experiments.
source: Three to five days, CantonS males were used for dusting and spontaneous grooming experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: For optogenetic experiments, larvae were raised on normal food and after eclosion, 1-day-old adults were transferred into food containing 0.4 mM all-trans-retinal and reared in the dark for another 2 days.
source: For optogenetic experiments, larvae were raised on normal food. After eclosion, 1-day-old adults were transferred into food containing 0.4 mM all-trans-retinal and reared in the dark for another 2 days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Behavior videos were recorded inside New Brunswick I2400 incubator shaker or DigiTherm DT2-MP-47L heating/cooling incubator.
source: Behavior videos were recorded inside New Brunswick I2400 incubator shaker or DigiTherm DT2-MP-47L heating/cooling incubator.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Experiments were performed every 2°C between 18°C and 30°C.
source: Experiments were performed every 2°C between 18°C and 30°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: 60 Hz videos were recorded for 9 min in optogenetics experiments, 13 min in dusting, and spontaneous grooming experiments with a FLIR Blackfly S USB3 camera.
source: 60 Hz videos were recorded for 9 min in optogenetics experiments, 13 min in dusting, and spontaneous grooming experiments with a FLIR Blackfly S USB3 camera.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: 8–12 flies were used per temperature or per experimental group for all experiments.
source: For all experiments described above, 8–12 flies were used per temperature or per experimental group (for the TNT inhibition experiment).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
